title: ui-agent-v6 camera-direction LoRA
description:
Task-1508 measured what MiniMax H3 actually does when you direct the camera: all 20 moves in MiniMax's published vocabulary, 32 cinematography techniques it publishes no word for, and 8 controls, plus 11 re-tests. 71 clips, every one watched, scored on two independent gates (measured motion + watched quality).

Results: /labs?study=h3camera
TDD: /notebook?noteId=50bfba6c-bb2e-40ac-9ea4-3bc9b3da20b0

Turn that into a ui-agent LoRA so the agent writes world-class camera direction by default, the same way v3 learned H3's prompt format and v5 learned reference/extend/v2v. Follow the shape of task-1491, task-1494 and task-1507.

WHAT THE STUDY FOUND, and what the LoRA has to teach:

1. Techniques H3 has NO published word for pass at 69%; the 20 words it documents pass at 40%. Our shipped @h3-video-prompt tells the agent to use only those 20 words and explicitly forbids the rest ("do not invent moves like dolly zoom or crane down"). That instruction is wrong for cranes, fisheye, whip pan, foreground wipe, crash zoom, orbit, top-down, ground-level and the whole subject-relationship family, all of which work.

2. BUT when a move IS one of the 20 words, the word beats a paraphrase: "Push In with small amplitude at slow speed" gave x1.053 with parallax; a plain "slow dolly in" gave 36 px. Rule: use the word if it exists, describe it in plain English if it does not, never paraphrase a word that exists.

3. Amplitude and speed are the strongest lever and are technique-specific. Tilt Up: 21 px at small amplitude, 737 px at large - 35x on one word. Pan Left: 1.3x on the same word. The agent must set amplitude deliberately per technique, not default everything to "small amplitude at slow speed".

4. Dead words that should be avoided or substituted: Pedestal Up and Pedestal Down (nothing at either amplitude - use a described crane instead), POV, Shake Slightly, Shake Strongly, handheld, pendulum, held dutch angle, dolly zoom, aperture/depth-of-field. H3 executes monotonic travel; it will not oscillate, will not hold a state it has to travel into, and will not add instability.

5. Say what the audience SEES, never what the operator does to the equipment. Every instruction phrased as a camera setting failed; the same idea phrased as a visible consequence succeeded.

6. First-frame mode pins frame 0 to the reference still, so describe travelling TO a state, never opening IN it. "Climbs until it is looking straight down" works; "opens directly overhead" does not.

7. Multi-shot works: cuts land on the specified timecode and each [Shot N] block keeps its own camera behaviour. Two cuts inside five seconds is fine.

8. Warn about the cost: the bigger the camera move, the less identity survives. Every large move in the study came back with a visibly different woman.

STEPS:

1. Author the dataset in the Text LoRA Datasets UI page on PROD. That page is the only allowed source of training data - never files on disk, never harvested from conversations, never dev.
2. Hand-write gold items from the study's 17 gold wordings and the 8 rules above, including negative examples (what the agent should NOT promise) so it stops offering pedestals, dutch holds and dolly zooms.
3. Combine with the existing ui-agent datasets, as the earlier ui-agent LoRAs do.
4. Train on the WSL Unsloth trainer, export a runtime adapter GGUF, serve it in llama.cpp, add it to the UI-agent brain selector.
5. Grade before vs after on held-out camera briefs - "give me a vertigo shot on the salt flats", "crane up and off the rooftop", "rack focus from the palms onto her", "whip pan away from her" - and confirm no regression against the earlier ui-agent suites.
6. Set it as default once it matches or beats v5 elsewhere and clearly beats it on camera direction.

Also in scope for this ticket, because it is a production change task-1508 deliberately did not make: revise @h3-video-prompt itself so it stops forbidding out-of-vocabulary techniques, teaches the rules above, and sets amplitude per technique.

Do not invent camera claims the study did not measure. Every number is n=1 per cell - the same Truck Right instruction measured 8, 79 and 2423 px across three cells - so treat the study's numbers as indicative of what a technique CAN do, never as a success rate.

title: Nine model files on J: are silently corrupt — whole weight tensors are zero, and the file size still matches
description:
Found while diagnosing task-1927. The Krea 2 RedCraft checkpoint returns pure noise because 69 of its 256 weight tensors are entirely zero and about a third of the file is a zero region — while its size matches the publisher's listing to the byte. Scanning every safetensors file under `J:/llm-models/ComfyUI_windows_portable/ComfyUI/models` for the same signature finds it is not alone.

**The scanner is `_agent_output/task-1927-redcraft-noise/scan-zeros.mjs`.** It reads the safetensors header, checks the offsets are contiguous and match the file size, then samples six windows spread across every tensor over 1 MB and reports the ones that are entirely zero. It skips LoRA `lora_up`/`lora_A` factors, which are legitimately zero-initialised — counting those made its first run flag nine healthy LoRA files.

**Corrupt, excluding RedCraft itself (which task-1927 replaces):**

| File | Zeroed weight tensors | Size |
|---|---|---|
| `diffusion_models/wan2.2_i2v_high_noise_14B_fp16.safetensors` | 122 | 28.6 GB |
| `diffusion_models/wan2.2_i2v_high_noise_14B_fp8_scaled.safetensors` | 241 | 14.3 GB |
| `diffusion_models/wan2.2_i2v_low_noise_14B_fp16.safetensors` | 306 | 28.6 GB |
| `diffusion_models/wan2.2_i2v_low_noise_14B_fp8_scaled.safetensors` | 365 | 14.3 GB |
| `checkpoints/ltx-2.3-22b-dev.safetensors` | 726 | 46.1 GB |
| `text_encoders/umt5_xxl_fp8_e4m3fn_scaled.safetensors` | 154 | 6.7 GB |
| `text_encoders/qwen_3_8b.safetensors` | 77 | 16.4 GB |
| `text_encoders/gemma-3-12b-abliterated-text-encoder.safetensors` | 68 | 23.5 GB |
| `text_encoders/ernie/ministral-3-3b.safetensors` | 274 | 7.7 GB |

Every one of them reports a correct file size and contiguous tensor offsets, so nothing has ever raised an error.

**All of these are referenced by shipped workflows**, which is what makes this worth acting on rather than filing away:
- `wan2.2_i2v_high/low_noise_14B_fp8_scaled` — `createWan22V2vWorkflow.ts`, `wan2.2-i2v-audio.json`
- `wan2.2_i2v_high/low_noise_14B_fp16` — `extended_video_v11.json`
- `umt5_xxl_fp8_e4m3fn_scaled` — `createScailImageToVideoWorkflow.ts`, `createWan22EnhancedImageToVideoWorkflow.ts`, `createWan22V2vWorkflow.ts`, `extended_video_v11.json`, `jason-svi-incognito-v3.json`, `wan2.2-i2v-audio.json`
- `ltx-2.3-22b-dev` — the LTX 2.3 workflows

**The finding was verified three independent ways, not inferred from one sampled read:**
1. Reading `blocks.10.self_attn.q.weight` of `wan2.2_i2v_low_noise_14B_fp16.safetensors` **in full** — all 52,428,800 bytes — returns zero non-zero bytes, while its neighbour `blocks.10.self_attn.k.weight` in the same file is 99.79% non-zero. An attention query projection cannot legitimately be zero next to a healthy key projection.
2. PowerShell reading the same byte range with a plain `FileStream` agrees, so it is not a Node read-path problem. `fsutil sparse queryflag` says the file is NOT sparse, so these are zeros actually written to disk.
3. `umt5_xxl_fp8_e4m3fn_scaled.safetensors` is 6,735,906,897 bytes, exactly the size Comfy-Org publishes — and its SHA-256 is `dbce131d2cfee3d0b9864ca9a909c3355f98262d8fc31d6c9def0552e647c93b` against the published `c3355d30191f1f066b26d93fba017ae9809dce6c627dda5f6a66eaa651204f68`. Same size, different content.

**What this ticket should do:**
1. Work out the cause before re-downloading anything, or it will happen again. All eight physical disks report `Status OK` through WMI, but the SMART predict-failure query needs elevation and was not answered — run it elevated. Check the J: volume's dirty bit and run `chkdsk /scan J:` (both `fsutil fsinfo volumeinfo J:` and `fsutil dirty query J:` returned `Access is denied` unelevated). Look at whether these files share a copy or move operation in their history — several have a December 2025 mtime.
2. Re-download the nine files (about 186 GB) and **verify each against the publisher's SHA-256**, not against its size. Size is what made every one of these look fine.
3. Re-run `scan-zeros.mjs` over the whole model tree afterwards and confirm it comes back clean.
4. Consider promoting the scanner into the repo (`backend/scripts/`) and running it after any bulk model copy, since the failure is silent and the symptom — a model that quietly produces worse output — is the kind nobody attributes to the file.

**Note the symptom is not always obvious.** RedCraft was 27% zeroed and returned pure noise. A text encoder missing a third of its weights does not fail; it produces weaker conditioning, which reads as "the model is ignoring my prompt" rather than as a broken file.

title: The write gate fails closed on every workload: side_table.note disagrees with SQLite by 3420
description:
**`inillucent-writegate` reports `gate: NOT MET` on all eight write and transaction workloads, so no write ratio can be taken on this box today.** Found while re-measuring for task-2024; it is not caused by that ticket's change, which was reverted and re-run to prove it.

## The failure

```sh
cargo build --release -p inillucent-compat --bin inillucent-writegate
target/release/inillucent-writegate <medium fixture> --rounds 30 --page-size 32768 --frames 4096
```

```
write.insert.batch  -  -  -  NO: round 0:
  inillucent ["100000|5102110000|2147672494384|2142775731856", "25100|315017550|105546107990|261865", "500|125250|22890"]
  sqlite     ["100000|5102110000|2147672494384|2142775731856", "25100|315017550|105546107990|258445", "500|125250|22890"]
```

## What is known

- **One of the nine numbers differs**: `sum(length(note))` on `side_table`, **261865 against 258445**, a difference of **3420**. The second agreement question is `SELECT count(*), sum(id), sum(owner), sum(length(note)) FROM side_table` and its first three fields agree, so both arms end with the same rows carrying the same ids and owners. The text in them differs.
- **No workload is refused** on either arm, so it is not one engine skipping a statement.
- **Not a dirty fixture.** Three separate copies - `_agent_output/fixtures/medium.db`, `_agent_output/gate-fixtures/medium.db` and `medium-run1.db` - each produce eight disagreements. SQLite reads the fixture at rest as 25,000 rows, no nulls, every `note` of type `text`, `sum(length(note))` 238894.
- Every workload prints the same digest pair, because the agreement questions are asked once per round after all eight have run. So the difference belongs to the round rather than to one workload, from this output alone.
- The gate is behaving correctly by refusing - that is `gates_fail_closed` doing its job. What is wrong is upstream of it.

## Where to start

The workloads that write `note` are `write.insert.autocommit` (`INSERT INTO side_table(owner, note)`, 100 rows, `Bind::Text`) and the three `txn` workloads (`UPDATE side_table SET note = ?2 WHERE id = ?1`, `Bind::Scatter` for the id), one of which carries a `pre` of `UPDATE side_table SET note = 'note ' || id`. `Bind::Text` is `format!("row {iteration} lorem ipsum dolor sit amet consectetur")`, so a length difference means either a different set of rows was updated or a different string was written.

Run one round, keep `%TEMP%/inillucent-writegate-<pid>/ours.db` and `theirs.db`, and diff `SELECT id, note FROM side_table` between them - that names the rows in one query.

Check whether a `pre` statement runs a different number of times on the two arms: the new engine runs the workloads in process and the SQLite arm runs them through `sqlite-bench` from a plan file, and that is the one place the two could disagree about how often something runs.

## Why it matters

`docs/performance.md` and `docs/roadmap.md` both quote `write.insert.batch` at 0.72x and the `write` family at 2.12x. Those are gate figures, and the gate will not produce one until this is fixed - so the write family has no reproducible number right now, and roadmap item 2 cannot be graded.

Evidence from the task-2024 run: `_agent_output/task-2024-splice/writegate-before.txt` (the change reverted) and `writegate-after.txt` (the change in place), which are identical in their disagreement.

title: embed(TEXT) with no model installed says "bad parameter or other API misuse" instead of naming setup-embeddings
description:
Found while verifying 0.1.2 on a machine that had never run `inillucent setup-embeddings` (task-1934). The published Linux archive, on a fresh WSL install:

```
$ inillucent --db probe.rdb query "SELECT length(embed('hello'))" --output json
{
  "ok": false,
  "command": "query",
  "status": "syntax",
  "message": "bad parameter or other API misuse",
  "text": "Error [syntax]: bad parameter or other API misuse"
}
```

`crates/inillucent-search/src/embed.rs` builds a different message for exactly this case:

```rust
fn no_model() -> error::DbError {
    error::misuse(format!(
        "embed: no embedding model is installed. Run `inillucent setup-embeddings` to download ..."
```

and the file's own test asserts `message.contains("inillucent setup-embeddings")`. So the message exists and the test passes, and the text a person actually sees is the generic one for the `misuse` status. Something between the scalar function and the CLI is printing the status's stock text rather than the error's own message.

This matters more now than it did before 0.1.2. Until 0.1.2 the published archives had no `embed` at all, so the answer was `no such function: embed`, which at least named the function. Now the function is there and the weights are not until somebody runs one command, and that is the state every new installation starts in. `agent-skills/inillucent-search/SKILL.md` promises the better behaviour in so many words: *"a build with it but no model installed refuses by name and tells you the command that installs one"*.

Two things to work out:

1. Where the message is dropped. `SELECT length(embed('hello'))` against a binary with the feature and no model is the whole reproduction; installing the model with `inillucent setup-embeddings all` and re-running returns `3072`, which is how the cause was narrowed to the no-model path.
2. Whether `syntax` is the right status for it. A missing model is not a syntax error, and `misuse` is what the code raises.

**Also worth checking while in there**, and not verified as a defect: `inillucent functions` lists no `embed`, on a Windows and a Linux 0.1.2 binary that both answer `SELECT length(embed('hello'))` with `3072`. If the register is meant to describe what the running build can do, a feature-gated function that answers but is not listed is a gap; if the register is deliberately the static set, that is fine and only worth a sentence saying so.

title: The score card prints 38,977 documents for a corpus that has 38,847
description:
`inillucent-scorecard.md`'s header line comes from `index.commit()` -> `BuildStats.documents` -> `Store::n_documents()`, which is `self.documents.len()`. On the graded synthetic corpus it reads **38,977**. The corpus has **38,847**, and so does the PostgreSQL baseline loaded from the same file, so the store is holding 130 document entries that do not correspond to a document.

**Proven three ways against the same `J:/inillucent-embeddings/corpus.jsonl`:**

- distinct `doc_id` across its 185,078 lines: **38,847**
- distinct `(source, doc_id)` pairs: **38,847**, and no `doc_id` appears under more than one source, so it is not a key-width question
- `select count(*) from documents` in `inillucent_synth`: **38,847**, with zero documents holding no chunk

It is not a count of contiguous runs of equal `doc_id` either - that is also 38,847.

**It is a regression.** The score card generated at commit 0c14f71d printed `185078 chunks across 38847 documents`. The card generated today at e2a81e1 prints `185078 chunks across 38977 documents` from the same cache file, which has not been rewritten since 2026-08-30. The chunk count is right in both.

Only the card's header sentence reads this number, so no graded measurement depends on it, and every comparison on the card reproduced the earlier run's figures exactly. It is still a published number that is wrong, and `Store::n_documents` is what a caller would use to ask how many documents an index holds.

Found while re-running the retrieval grading for task-1935. Evidence and the run transcripts are in `_agent_output/task-1935-regrade2/` and the run directory `J:/inillucent-embeddings/runs/1789828186-e2a81e10/`.

title: plan_cache fails at random: its scratch file is named by process id, against 1,125 leftovers
description:
Found by task-1973's `inillucent-testrun --changed --strict` run: 190 targets, 3,041 tests, **1 failed** - `inillucent-compat::plan_cache`, 6 of its 7 tests, all at `crates/inillucent-compat/tests/plan_cache.rs:53` with

```
CREATE TABLE t(a INTEGER): DbError { extended: ExtendedCode(1),
  context: Some(ErrorContext { message: Some("table t already exists"), ... }) }
```

It is not a real failure and it is not task-1973's: that ticket touched `crates/inillucent-bench/src`, two `crates/inillucent-compat/tests` files that are not this one, three documents, `tools/doc-facts/check.mjs` and the baseline amendments - nothing `plan_cache` compiles against. Re-run on its own it passes **7/7, three times in a row**.

## Why it fails

`plan_cache.rs`'s fixture:

```rust
fn scratch(name: &str) -> std::path::PathBuf {
    let root = inillucent_compat::workspace_root()
        .join("_agent_output/plan-cache")
        .join(name);
    std::fs::create_dir_all(&root).expect("the scratch directory");
    static NEXT: std::sync::atomic::AtomicU32 = std::sync::atomic::AtomicU32::new(0);
    let serial = NEXT.fetch_add(1, std::sync::atomic::Ordering::Relaxed);
    root.join(format!("{}-{serial}.db", std::process::id()))
}
```

and the comment above the `open` it feeds:

```
// A fresh file per run: the process id is in the name, so a second run does
// not inherit the first one's schema and nothing has to be removed.
```

That claim does not hold. The file is never removed, so `_agent_output/plan-cache/` accumulates one per test per run - **1,125 `.db` files today**, the oldest dated 2026-09-09, 144 in each of the seven per-test directories across 143 distinct process ids. Windows reuses process ids, and the `serial` a given test receives depends on which of the six-to-eight test threads reaches `scratch()` first, so the `{pid}-{serial}.db` a test asks for is not stable between runs either. When a run's pair collides with a leftover, `Database::open_with_busy_timeout` opens the old file and its schema, and the fixture's `CREATE TABLE t` fails on the table the previous run left behind.

The failing run's own signature says exactly that: the six directories whose tests failed still carried their **2026-09-17 21:56** modification time afterwards, because no new file was created in them - the file already existed. `function_registration`, the one test that passed, is the one directory whose modification time moved to the time of the run.

## What to change

The fixture, not the leftovers. Two candidates, either is enough:

1. **Remove the file, or the directory, at the start of the test.** The comment says "nothing has to be removed" as though that were a property worth having; it is the cause. A `remove_file` that ignores `NotFound` before `open` makes each test's starting point the one it asserts against.
2. **Name the file with something that cannot repeat** - a nanosecond timestamp beside the process id, or `tempfile`-style uniqueness - and delete it on the way out. Note that a per-test `AtomicU32` would not fix this on its own, because the collision needs only the process id to repeat.

Whichever it is, the comment above `open` has to stop claiming freshness the code does not provide. That is rule 1.5 of `tests/inillucent-testing-tdd.md`: a comment may only claim what its test proves.

While in there, check whether any other suite names a scratch path by process id alone. `grep -rn 'process::id' crates/*/tests crates/*/src/bin` is the search.

## The 1,125 files

They are in `_agent_output/plan-cache/`, which is gitignored, and they are about 140 MB. task-1973 did not delete them: they were not created by it, and an agent does not delete files it did not create. **Recommend removing the whole `_agent_output/plan-cache/` directory** once the fixture is fixed - every file in it is a dead scratch database from a finished test run, and leaving them is what keeps the collision live.

Do it after the fixture change, not before, or the next run starts the pile again.

title: Inillucent: importing a SQLite database whose column is named `left` reports the file as corrupt
description:
Found while building task-1814 (the Unluminous database explorer's Inillucent support). Two faults in one reproduction, and the second is the worse of them.

## Reproduce

```rust
// a perfectly ordinary SQLite database, written by SQLite itself
let s = rusqlite::Connection::open("reserved.db")?;
s.execute_batch("create table pairs (left text, right text); insert into pairs values ('a','b');")?;

inillucent_driver::Database::import_sqlite("reserved.db")
// -> status = Corrupt, message = "database disk image is malformed"
```

The same import of a database with no reserved-word column succeeds:

```
import plain:    ok -> plain.db.rdb
import reserved: FAILED status=Corrupt message="database disk image is malformed"
```

And the same word is refused directly by the engine's own parser:

```
create table pairs (left text, right text)
-> Syntax: near "left": syntax error, expected a name
```

## Why it matters

**1. `left` and `right` are ordinary column names in SQLite.** They are not reserved there - SQLite's keyword list lets `LEFT` be an identifier in this position, and real schemas use both (a diff table, a tree, a stereo channel, a page layout). The dialect is supposed to be SQLite's, so a schema SQLite accepts and this engine refuses is a parity gap rather than a caller's mistake. `inillucent-sql`'s lexer/parser is presumably treating the join keywords as unconditionally reserved.

**2. The diagnosis is wrong, and that is the part that costs somebody an afternoon.** `database disk image is malformed` says the file is damaged. The file is not damaged - SQLite reads it perfectly - and somebody chasing that message will go looking for corruption, run `PRAGMA integrity_check` on a healthy database, and find nothing. Whatever the underlying cause, an import that cannot parse a `CREATE` statement should say which statement and why, in the way the engine already does elsewhere: `Unsupported` with the construct named, or `Syntax` with the word.

The engine is otherwise unusually good about this - `VACUUM` answers `Unsupported` with `feature: "VACUUM"`, and an outer join answered `"the new engine's physical pass does not handle an outer join yet"` - which is exactly why this one stands out.

## Where to look

- `crates/inillucent-sql` - the name/keyword rule for a column position.
- `crates/inillucent-engine`'s import path (`ImportedDatabase::import_with` -> `table_from_create_sql`), for how a parse failure there becomes `Corrupt`.
- `drivers/conformance/suite.json` is the place to add the case once it is fixed: a table whose columns are named `left` and `right`, imported and read back.

## Not a defect, recorded so it is not re-investigated

`select * from docs` on an `inillucent_search` table answers `["title", "body"]` and omits the hidden `vector` column. That is FTS5's own behaviour and is right; Unluminous names the column explicitly, the way it already names SQLite's rowid.

title: inillucent-bench embed-check: a cache fails a verification that re-embedding cannot clear
description:
`embed-check` failed a cache on task-1966 and told the operator to do something that provably does not change the outcome. Found while building a corpus-small cache of `nomic-embed-text-v2-moe`; the numbers below are all measured on this box.

## What it reports

```
vector length:                n=18685 min=1.000000 ... max=1.000000, 0 not unit length
vectors of the wrong width:   0
cosine(stored, re-embedded):  n=2000 min=0.999409 p5=0.999985 p50=0.999998 mean=0.999995 max=1.000000
1 of 2000 sampled vectors do not match their text, worst first:
  chunk 11574 (github, 591 chars): cosine 0.9994
Error: the cache pairs text with vectors that were not made from it by nomic-embed-text-v2-moe.
       Rerun synth-embed after deleting the vectors file, or rebuild the corpus and embed it again
```

## Why the message is wrong

The cache was rebuilt from zero, 18,685 chunks, a fresh `llama-server`, nothing reused. The second verification is **identical to six figures**: same `min=0.999409`, same `p5`, `p50`, `mean`, `max`, and **the same chunk 11574 at the same cosine 0.9994**. So the remedy the error names - rerun `synth-embed` after deleting the vectors file - was carried out in full and produced an equivalent result. An operator following the message loops.

## What it is not

- **Not nondeterminism.** Jitter would have moved the minimum to a different chunk across two independent builds. It did not move at all.
- **Not batch shape.** The build runs `--batch 128` and the check `--batch 16`, so that was the obvious candidate. Measured against the server directly: chunk 11574 embedded twice alone is **1.000000**, and batch 16 against batch 128 is **0.999998**. That is 2e-6 for this chunk against the 6e-4 the check reports. Across 16 neighbouring chunks the worst batch-16-against-128 cosine is 0.999844, so the effect is real but an order of magnitude too small.
- **Not the text.** Chunk 11574 is 591 characters of Python import statements, pure ASCII, no characters above U+007F, nowhere near the 512 token bound the same run reports 56 of 2000 chunks exceeding.
- **Not a corrupt cache.** All 18,685 vectors are unit length to six figures and none is the wrong width.

## Why it matters beyond one chunk

The bar sits between **0.999409 and 0.999657** - the second number is the minimum of task-1966's full-corpus cache of the same model, built the same way, which passes. Two caches of one model on one box land either side of the threshold on the strength of a single sampled chunk, and the check's verdict is binary.

Quantified impact, both caches graded through an identical `grade-embedding` command: dense six-family composite **0.6531 against 0.6532**, hybrid **0.8986 against 0.8986**. One ten-thousandth, which is a hundredth of the 0.01 practical threshold the card declares.

## What is wanted

Not a raised threshold as a first move - task-1966 deliberately did not touch it, because changing a bar so one's own artefact passes is the wrong instinct and the finding was worth more than a clean line. What is wanted is:

1. **Find out what actually differs for chunk 11574**, since it is reproducible and therefore findable. The candidates not yet eliminated are how `synth-embed` presents text to the server against how `embed-check` does - a prefix, a normalisation, a truncation, or a difference in how the request is split under `--max-batch-cells`.
2. **Make the message honest.** Whatever the bar ends up being, an error must not prescribe a remedy that cannot clear it. If a reproducible per-chunk difference is expected, say so and say what would clear it.
3. **Decide what the check is for.** If it is guarding against text paired with another text's vectors, a single chunk at 0.9994 among 1,999 above 0.99998 is not that failure, and a bound on the *distribution* would catch the real one better than a bound on the minimum.

## Where the evidence is

- `J:/inillucent-embeddings/task-1966/caches/v2moe-small.cache` and `.vectors` - the rebuild
- `J:/inillucent-embeddings/task-1966/caches/v2moe-small-run1.cache` and `.vectors` - the first build, kept for comparison
- `_agent_output/task-1966-embedding-v2/phase0/verify-v2moe-small.log` and `.log.run1` - the two verifications
- `_agent_output/task-1966-embedding-v2/teacher-on-corpus-small/` - both gradings
- task-1966's board comments at the time of the rebuild carry the reasoning

title: inillucent: txn.large lost 10% and read.join's lower bound slipped under 3.00x when the delta area grew (task-2074)
description:
task-2074 sized a leaf's delta area by the free gap instead of capping it at 32 rows, and added the compaction splice. On `inillucent-fullgate` (medium fixture, 32 KiB page, 30 rounds, base and new alternated twice in a quiet window) the write family went from 2.43x/2.33x to 3.28x/3.24x and `write.insert.batch` from 0.88x/0.81x to 1.52x/1.52x. Two things got worse, and this ticket is for them. The numbers and the reasoning are in `docs/performance.md`, section "The cost of each secondary index, on the index count sweep", and the four gate outputs are in `C:/jason/dev/inillucent/_agent_output/task-2074-delta-gap/gate-*.txt`.

## 1. `txn.large` is 10% slower, consistently

Base 4.06x and 4.15x, after 3.84x and 3.59x. `txn.large` is 2,000 `UPDATE side_table SET note = ?` that lengthen a text in place. `LeafMut::overwrite_heap_slot` makes room for the longer value with `carve_heap`, which moves the tombstone bitmap and the whole delta area down by the value's size (`crates/inillucent-tree/src/mutate.rs`). The area is now as large as the free gap rather than 32 rows, so each move copies more.

A place to start: carve the new value from the gap below the delta area (between the mini-columns and the bitmap) instead of moving the area, which needs the heap to allow a value outside `[heap_start, page_size)` - or compact first when the area is past some size. Whatever changes, `carve_room` and `carve_heap` must still agree and stay deterministic, because recovery replays `UpdateInPlace` by running them again; `crates/inillucent-model/tests/redo_bytes.rs` compares every page byte for byte after a crash and must stay green.

## 2. `read.join`'s lower bound went from 3.14x/3.04x to 2.92x/2.98x against a 3.00x bar

`join.range` moved from 0.90x/0.87x to 0.87x/0.84x. That is about as much as the two base runs differ from each other, so first establish whether it is real: more rounds, both arms alternated, in a quiet window. If it is, the likely cause is that a leaf written to during the round keeps more delta rows for longer, and a range probe into such a leaf merges them (`LeafRef::live_between` calls `live`, which materialises the whole leaf). `live_matching` already merges only the probe's run; `live_between` could do the same with `delta_matching`-style bounds.

Done means: both measured in a quiet window against the task-2074 commit as the base, with the numbers in `docs/performance.md`, and neither change undoing task-2074's write gains.

title: inillucent: an index join into an untyped column returns no rows
description:
Found by task-2078 while checking `UPDATE ... FROM` with `INDEXED BY`. **Not dispatched** - filed for the supervisor.

## What is wrong

An index nested loop join whose inner side is an index on a column with no declared type (BLOB affinity) returns **no rows**, when the probe value comes from another table's column. The rows are wrong, not only the plan. The installed release build (`C:/Users/jason/AppData/Local/Programs/inillucent/bin/inillucent-shell`) does the same, so this is on `main` and not a task-2078 change.

```sql
CREATE TABLE h1(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, a); INSERT INTO h1 VALUES (1,3); CREATE INDEX h1_a ON h1(a);
CREATE TABLE h2(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, a INTEGER); INSERT INTO h2 VALUES (1,3); CREATE INDEX h2_a ON h2(a);
CREATE TABLE s1(k); INSERT INTO s1 VALUES (3);
CREATE TABLE s2(k INTEGER); INSERT INTO s2 VALUES (3);
SELECT count(*) FROM s1, h1 WHERE h1.a = s1.k;   -- 0 here, 1 in sqlite 3.53.4
SELECT count(*) FROM s2, h1 WHERE h1.a = s2.k;   -- 0 here, 1 in sqlite
SELECT count(*) FROM s1, h2 WHERE h2.a = s1.k;   -- 1, correct
SELECT count(*) FROM h1 WHERE a = 3;             -- 1, correct
SELECT count(*) FROM h1 WHERE a = (SELECT k FROM s1); -- 1, correct
```

Without the index, or with `NOT INDEXED` on `h1`, the join answers correctly. `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` is `SCAN s1` then `SEARCH h1 USING INDEX h1_a (a=?)`, the same as SQLite. So the defect is in how the probe value is turned into a seek key when the indexed column has BLOB affinity and the value is read from an outer row. A guess to check first: an affinity or type tag applied to the key that the stored entry does not have.

It also breaks `UPDATE t SET ... FROM s WHERE t.a = s.k` on untyped columns: the update changes nothing and reports success.

## Done means

- The five statements above match the pinned shell.
- A test in `crates/inillucent-compat` that joins through an index on an untyped column, graded against the reference, with the typed and untyped combinations above. Every one of these currently passes as long as a column in the pair has a declared type, which is probably why nothing caught it.

title: task-2043's page-free-at-commit corrupts a database at a 4 KiB page with a 64 frame pool
description:
**task-2043's fix corrupts a database at a 4,096 byte page with a 64 frame pool.** Found by task-2036's Nikaya startup story, which runs the same sequence at six configurations.

## What happens

`crates/inillucent/tests/story_nikaya.rs::a_startup_migration_leaves_every_neighbour_readable` runs Nikaya's startup migration against a populated database: create the migration ledger, ask it what has run, create a table, `ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN` on a populated one, index the column it added, record the migration. Then it closes the database and opens it again.

At the **small-pool** arm - `page_size = 4096`, `frames = 64` - the reopen fails:

```
nikaya.rdb is not sound after a reopen at the small-pool arm: database disk image is malformed
```

The other five arms pass, including `sqlite-page`, which is the same 4,096 byte page with the default 4,096 frame pool. **So it needs the small pool, not the small page.** It reproduces every run.

## Which commit, measured

`65fece6` - *task-2043: a page a transaction drops is freed at its commit, not before*.

Checking out that commit's parent for the eight engine files it touched (`ddl.rs`, `ddl/alter.rs`, `ddl/catalog.rs`, `ddl/tree.rs`, `engine/batch.rs`, `engine/compiled.rs`, `engine/state.rs`, `marks.rs`) and rebuilding makes the story pass; restoring them makes it fail again. Nothing else in the tree changed between the two runs.

## Why the pool size matters, probably

64 frames at 4,096 bytes is a 256 KB pool - small enough that the migration's pages are evicted and re-read while the transaction that freed them is still open. A page that is freed at commit rather than when the statement runs is live for longer, and a pool that cannot hold it is where the two meet. That is a guess about the mechanism; the measurement above is not.

## The reproduction

```sh
cargo test -p inillucent --test story_nikaya a_startup_migration_leaves_every_neighbour_readable::small_pool
```

The arm is `Arm { page_size: 4096, frames: 64 }` from `crates/inillucent-compat/src/matrix.rs`; `Database::open_at(path, 4096, 64)` is the whole of the configuration.

## What done looks like

1. The mechanism, named: which page is read back wrong, and why the free at commit is what does it.
2. The fix, with `story_nikaya` green at all six arms.
3. Take the line out of `tests/workloads/nikaya/story.allow.list`, which is where task-2036 wrote it off. An entry that no longer describes a failure is itself a failure, so the story goes red until the line goes.
4. Worth asking whether `durability.rs`'s new cases from task-2043 run at anything other than the default pool. They pass at 4,096 frames and this does not.

title: inillucent: a family's lower bound measures the gap between its workloads; fix the statistic, then re-decide read.join's 3.00x bar
description:
**The defect.** fullgate, readgate, writegate and scorecard all compute a family's 95% interval by putting every workload's every round into one list and bootstrapping the mean of that list. A resample draws the workloads in random proportions. When a family's workloads differ, that proportion moves the mean far more than timing noise does. `read.join` shows it most clearly: `join.selective` reads about 21x and `join.range` about 0.87x, each measured to within 2%, and the family interval is [2.76x, 6.67x]. The printed bound can be predicted from the two workload ratios alone, as exp(m - 1.96 x (d/2) / sqrt(60)), to within 0.07x on every clean pass at every build task-2086 measured. It affects every family with more than one workload.

**A fix exists and is not merged.** Branch `task-2086-family-interval`, commit `3f7c0bf` (also `_agent_output/task-2086-read-join/family-interval.patch`). `perf::family_interval` computes one value per round, the mean of that round's log ratios over the family's workloads, and bootstraps rounds. That is the statistic `weighted_headline` already uses for each family. All four programs use it. It has two tests. Pinned, `read.join` reads 4.15x [4.11, 4.21] and 4.17x [4.16, 4.25]. Before merging, re-measure every family under both statistics and publish the change for each one. The bounds get narrower everywhere, so a family that passes only because of the change has to be named.

**Then the bar.** 3.00x for `read.join` is the "low estimate" column of `tasks/task-1816-rearchitecture-tdd.md` line 735, in a table headed "Targets are estimates unless marked measured", written when the family read 0.154x. No one ever measured it. Under the current statistic, pinned, the full plan never cleared it at any build: `b0ba286` read 2.20x and 2.38x because `join.selective` was 11x then, and HEAD reads 2.76x to 2.87x. Only the read gate's plan cleared it, at `57e87b0` and `b0ba286`, with 3.03x to 3.28x. Decide the bar under the corrected statistic, with the evidence written down. Do not lower it to match today.

## How it was measured

A detached worktree needs `git checkout -- Cargo.lock` before each checkout, or the checkout fails and the old binary is reused. Evidence and scripts: `C:/jason/dev/inillucent/_agent_output/task-2086-read-join/` (README.md, summary.txt). Found by task-2086; the write-up is the section "Why `read.join` misses its 3.00x bar, and when it last met it" in `docs/performance.md`.

title: An UPDATE that violates a secondary UNIQUE index is accepted, silently
inillucent: the schema function authorizer has no caller, so direct_only and trusted_schema are inert
description:
Found while implementing task-1969 section 7.4 under task-1970.

`Registry::authorize_function` in `crates/inillucent-ext/src/registry.rs` is the engine's whole
schema-function policy: it refuses a `direct_only` function from a schema outright, and refuses a
non-innocuous one unless `trusted_schema` is on. It is called by **nothing**:

```
grep -rn authorize_function crates/ drivers/ --include=*.rs
```

returns the definition, its two unit tests, and no other caller. So today a `CHECK` constraint, an
index expression, a generated column, a `DEFAULT`, a partial-index predicate, a view and a trigger
may all name any registered function, whatever its flags. `PRAGMA trusted_schema`, `innocuous` and
`direct_only` are a policy with a passing unit test and no effect on the engine.

Measured under task-1970: with `embed` registered `direct_only: true`,
`CREATE INDEX i ON note (embed(body))`, `CREATE TABLE t (b TEXT CHECK (length(embed(b)) > 0))` and a
generated column naming `embed` are all **accepted**.

**Why task-1970 did not fix it.** Enforcement has to go where the binder binds a schema expression,
and the binder has no notion of schema context - there is no flag to thread, and `AuthAction` is the
application's authorizer (the `sqlite3_set_authorizer` equivalent) rather than this policy.
Threading a call site through `CHECK`, `DEFAULT`, generated columns, index expressions,
partial-index predicates, views and triggers is substantial work in `crates/inillucent-sql/src/bind.rs`,
and task-1970's own description forbids touching that file outside one named exception, because A15
and the bind split are already queued as their own ticket.

**What task-1970 did do**, so this ticket starts from a working half:

- `embed` now registers with `..FunctionFlags::external()`, so its flags say what its doc comment
  always claimed.
- `UserFunction::external(name, arity, body)` exists, so a registrant has a constructor that means
  what the two doc comments describing `direct_only` as "the default for anything registered from
  outside" say. `FunctionFlags::default()` is every flag false and is the trap that caused this.
- `Registry::refused` builds its sentence with `with_message` rather than `with_detail`. That was the
  second half of task-1952's defect: the refusal read `SQL logic error` to a caller, because a detail
  is internal diagnostic text.
- Three cases in `crates/inillucent-search/src/embed.rs` assert the flags and the registry's answer
  for a schema and for a statement.

**What this ticket is.**

1. Give the binder a call site - schema or statement - and thread it through every schema expression:
   `DEFAULT`, `CHECK`, a generated column's expression, an index expression, a partial-index
   predicate, a view's body and a trigger's body.
2. Consult `Registry::authorize_function` at each, through whatever seam keeps `inillucent-sql` below
   `inillucent-ext` - most likely by extending `ExternalFunction` with the flags, since that struct
   already exists to tell the binder what it needs to know about a registered function and
   deliberately carries no body.
3. Check `authorize_module`, `authorize_extension` and `authorize_shadow_write` the same way. If any
   of them has no caller either, it has the same problem.
4. Bring back `crates/inillucent-compat/tests/embed_direct_only.rs`. It was written under task-1970
   with five SQL-level cases - index expression, `CHECK`, generated column, statement level, and a
   trusted schema - and removed because four of them fail against today's engine. Its row declared
   `features = ["inillucent-engine/embed"]` and no `onnx`, because every case is refused while the
   statement is bound and the model is never loaded.
5. `PRAGMA trusted_schema` reports OFF and `engine/pragma.rs` says "a schema object is never treated
   as trusted input here". If that is the intended stance, the `innocuous` half refuses every
   non-innocuous registered function in a schema once the authorizer runs, which is a wider behaviour
   change than the `embed` one and needs its own decision.

This is a security-shaped gap: the policy exists because a hostile schema is how a database file
attacks the process that opens it.

title: inillucent: a gate's family interval covers one pass; repeat passes move 1.5 to 5% more, so a verdict near a bar is not settled by one pass
description:
Found by task-2093 on 2026-09-23.

**What is true now.** Since task-2093 every gate grades a family with `perf::family_interval`: one value a round, the mean of that round's log ratios over the family's workloads, rounds resampled. That interval states how precisely one pass measured the family. It does not state what the next pass will read.

**The measurement.** Four pinned passes of `inillucent-fullgate` on `main` at `16c01a4` plus task-2093 (mask 0xC03C03, read back from the SQLite child, medium fixture, 30 rounds, quiet window). In eight of the ten families the family ratio moved between passes by more than the per round half width. `read.join` read 4.15x to 4.37x, 5.2% apart, with a per round half width of about 1.5%, so one pass's interval [4.08x, 4.21x] does not contain another pass's ratio of 4.37x. Something constant within a pass and different between passes moves every round of it together. Evidence: `C:/jason/dev/inillucent/_agent_output/task-2093-family-statistic/` (summary.txt, criteria.txt, tables.txt), and the section "How a family's interval is computed (task-2093)" in `docs/performance.md`.

**Why it matters.** A family whose per round bound is within about 5% of its bar can pass on one pass and miss on the next. `extension` is that family today: its per round bound read 1.54x, 1.67x, 1.60x and 1.54x against a 1.50x bar.

**What to decide.** Whether a gate verdict should come from several passes (the published figures already use four runs), or from a between pass allowance measured once and applied to a single pass, or from a per pass statistic that resamples something that varies between passes (for example restarting the SQLite child or the fixture copy per block of rounds). Measure the between pass spread per family before choosing, pinned, and write down before the passes what would make you reject your own choice. Do not change any bar to absorb the spread.

title: inillucent-driver-capi: conformance reports a strict skip whenever python_conformance runs beside it and the library needs relinking
description:
Found by task-2098. Not caused by it: the mechanism is in the two test files as they are on main.

`inillucent-testrun --target inillucent-driver-capi::conformance --target inillucent-driver-capi::python_conformance --strict --no-build` reported `conformance` as `FAILED ... 1 suite(s) ran without a prerequisite and evidenced nothing: needs cc, asan` in 5 of 5 runs. The same target run alone passed 2 of 2. `--changed --strict` hit it once in three runs.

The cause, reproduced directly: `python_conformance` loads `target/debug/inillucent_driver_capi.dll` into a Python process through ctypes. At the same time `conformance.rs`'s `build_library` runs `cargo build -p inillucent-driver-capi`. When that build has to relink (the runner's `cargo test` build and the plain `cargo build -p` have different fingerprints, so each one relinks after the other), cargo fails with `error: failed to remove file D:/agent-worktrees/cargo-target/inillucent-task-2098\debug\inillucent_driver_capi.dll ... Access is denied. (os error 5)`, because Windows will not remove a DLL another process has loaded. `build_library` then returns None and the test calls `skipping("the C ABI static library did not build")`, which `--strict` turns into a hollow failure.

Reproduction without the runner: load the DLL in Python (`python -c "import ctypes,time; ctypes.CDLL(r'<target>/debug/inillucent_driver_capi.dll'); time.sleep(90)"`), touch `drivers/inillucent-driver-capi/src/lib.rs`, and run `cargo build -p inillucent-driver-capi`. It exits 101 with the error above.

Two things to decide: how the two targets stop sharing the one DLL path (for example `conformance` linking the static library through a build that does not also relink the cdylib, or `python_conformance` copying the DLL to its own directory before loading it), and whether a failed `cargo build` in `build_library` should be a skip at all, since here it hid a real conflict as a missing prerequisite. The runner also does not print the output of a target it classifies as hollow, which is why this took a manual run to see.

title: A statement that fails partway keeps the rows it already wrote, and OR ROLLBACK does not roll back
description:
Found while working task-1849, **entirely on the pre-existing table-key path** — every repro below uses a table with no secondary `UNIQUE` index at all, so this is not that ticket's doing and is not in its scope. Measured against the pinned SQLite 3.53.4 oracle at `9d17ec0`.

## 1. There is no statement-scoped undo

SQLite's default conflict algorithm is ABORT, and ABORT means *the current statement's changes are undone and the transaction is kept*. This engine keeps them.

```sql
CREATE TABLE t(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, b INTEGER);
INSERT INTO t VALUES (1,1),(2,2),(12,3);
UPDATE t SET id=id+10 WHERE id<=2;
```

Row 1 moves to 11, row 2 collides with 12 and the statement fails. SQLite answers `1|1  2|2  12|3` and the error; this engine answers `11|1  2|2  12|3` and the error — half an `UPDATE`, committed, with a diagnostic that says it failed.

It is not specific to `UPDATE`, to the rowid, or to uniqueness. All of these differ the same way:

```sql
-- a multi-row INSERT whose second row collides
INSERT INTO t VALUES (9,0);
INSERT INTO t VALUES (1,1),(9,2);      -- sqlite: only 9 survives; ours: 9 and 1

-- NOT NULL, no index anywhere
CREATE TABLE t(a TEXT, b INTEGER NOT NULL);
INSERT INTO t VALUES ('p',1),('q',2);
UPDATE t SET a='r', b=CASE WHEN a='q' THEN NULL ELSE 5 END;
-- sqlite: both rows unchanged; ours: row 1 is now r|5

-- UPDATE OR REPLACE that deletes the row in the way and then fails a CHECK
CREATE TABLE t(a TEXT, b INTEGER CHECK(b < 9));
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX u ON t(a);
INSERT INTO t VALUES ('x',1),('y',2);
UPDATE OR REPLACE t SET a='x', b=20 WHERE b=2;
-- sqlite: both rows still there; ours: row x is gone, deleted by a statement that then failed
```

The last one is the worst shape of it: the failure **destroys** a row rather than half-writing one, and the statement reports an error, so nothing suggests looking.

## 2. `OR ROLLBACK` does not roll back the transaction

```sql
CREATE TABLE t(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, b INTEGER);
INSERT INTO t VALUES (1,1),(12,3);
BEGIN;
INSERT INTO t VALUES (99,9);
UPDATE OR ROLLBACK t SET id=id+11 WHERE id=1;
```

SQLite discards the whole transaction, so the `99` row is gone. This engine reports the constraint failure and keeps it. `exec.rs`/`dml.rs` map `ConflictAction::Rollback` onto `Resolution::Raise` with the comment that `ABORT`, `FAIL` and `ROLLBACK` "differ only in what the *session* undoes, which this layer does not own" — which is right about the layering and means the session layer has to be told, and is not.

All five algorithms actually differ, and only two of the differences are implemented today:

| algorithm | undoes the row | undoes the statement | undoes the transaction | today |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `IGNORE` | skips it, carries on | no | no | correct |
| `REPLACE` | resolves it, carries on | no | no | correct |
| `FAIL` | stops there, **keeps earlier rows** | no | no | correct by accident — it is the only one this engine's behaviour matches |
| `ABORT` (the default) | — | **yes** | no | **wrong** |
| `ROLLBACK` | — | yes | **yes** | **wrong** |

So `FAIL` and `ABORT` are currently indistinguishable, and ABORT is what every unqualified statement gets.

## What it will take

A statement-scoped undo point in the write path: open one before a DML statement writes anything, release it on success, roll back to it on a raise, and for `ROLLBACK` continue up to the transaction. The undo machinery already exists — `SAVEPOINT`/`ROLLBACK TO` and the ARIES-style undo records are in `inillucent-txn` — so this is about **where** the boundary is taken, not about building one.

The cost is what needs designing rather than assuming: every write statement would take and release an undo point, and `txn.large` is two thousand of them in one transaction. Measure before and after on a medium `inillucent-fullgate`; if a per-statement savepoint is too expensive, the cheaper shape is to record the undo LSN at statement start and roll forward to it only on the failure path, which costs one integer on the success path.

## Acceptance

- Each repro above answers as SQLite does, checked in `crates/inillucent-compat/tests/new_engine_writes.rs` (which applies each statement to both engines and re-probes every index against its table afterwards).
- `FAIL` and `ABORT` are distinguishable: a multi-row statement failing on its third row keeps the first two under `OR FAIL` and keeps none under the default.
- `OR ROLLBACK` discards the open transaction, and `autocommit` reads as SQLite's does afterwards — `dml_differential.rs`'s `compare` already checks that flag after every statement.
- `write.update.indexed`, `txn.large` and `txn.batched` stay inside the run-to-run spread on a medium `inillucent-fullgate`, with the numbers quoted.

Cases are in `_agent_output/task-1849-unique-update/cases3.json` (`b3.tablekey.partial.stmt`, `b3.tablekey.or.rollback`, `b3.ins.partial.stmt`, `b3.ins.tablekey.partial.stmt`, `b3.notnull.partial.stmt`, `b3.or.replace.check.fails`, `b3.or.replace.notnull.fails`) with the probe harness beside them.
